name: MDS211 SA2 Mock Exam 3
subtitle: Lectures 17–29 · Exam 2 / FA-SA2 Scope · 77 Questions
description: The third and most recent 77-question SA2 mock exam covering Lectures 17–29 (Motor System through Clinical Correlations), written directly from the MDS211 lecture slide decks rather than the past-paper archive, and weighted to match the official lecture-hour schedule. Every question has a single best answer among five options, with a full explanation covering both why the correct answer is right and the specific wrong-answer trap built into the distractors.

questions.stem: On the standard 0–5 grading scale for muscle power used in this course, a patient who can move a limb against gravity but cannot overcome any added resistance from the examiner is graded:
questions.explanation: The motor power scale runs 0 (no contraction) → 1 (trace of contraction) → 2 (cannot move against gravity) → 3 (moves against gravity but not against resistance) → 4 (reduced power against resistance) → 5 (normal power). Movement against gravity alone, with no resistance tolerated, is Grade 3. Common trap: Grade 4 is the tempting choice since it also involves “resistance,” but Grade 4 means the patient CAN partially resist the examiner — Grade 3 is specifically the point where gravity alone can be overcome but any added resistance defeats the movement.

questions.stem: A comatose patient shows bilateral arm flexion with wrist/finger flexion, and bilateral leg extension, in response to a painful stimulus. This decorticate posturing localizes the lesion to a level:
options: In the peripheral nerves and neuromuscular junctions, bilaterally
In the anterior horn motor neurons of the spinal cord, bilaterally
In the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, bilaterally
Above the level of the red nucleus (supratentorial)
At or below the level of the red nucleus (infratentorial)
questions.explanation: Decorticate rigidity (arms flexed, legs extended) results from a supratentorial lesion — damage at or above the internal capsule/basal ganglia level, sparing the rubrospinal-influenced flexor tone of the upper limbs. It is generally considered a less severe (though still serious) localization than decerebrate posturing. Common trap: It's easy to assume any “abnormal posturing” implies a low brainstem lesion, but decorticate posturing specifically points to a HIGHER (supratentorial) lesion — decerebrate posturing (arms AND legs extended) is the one that indicates a lower, infratentorial, and more dangerous lesion.

questions.stem: Motor units vary in size depending on how fine the required control is. Which of the following has the SMALLEST motor units, allowing the most precise, fine-grained control?
questions.explanation: Extraocular muscles have small motor units (few muscle fibers per motor neuron), which allows extremely fine, precise control of eye position — in contrast to large postural muscles like the trunk or legs, which use large motor units for powerful, coarser movements. Common trap: Trunk and leg muscles (B, C, D, E) are all large-postural-muscle examples that use LARGE motor units for power, not precision — don't let “big muscle” intuition override the actual size-vs-precision relationship being tested.

questions.stem: Which extrapyramidal descending tract facilitates the activity of flexor muscles of the limbs while inhibiting extensor muscle activity — the opposite pattern from the vestibulospinal tract?
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract, arising from the red nucleus, facilitates flexor muscle activity in the limbs and inhibits extensor activity — the mirror-image pattern to the vestibulospinal tract, which facilitates extensors and inhibits flexors to maintain antigravity posture. Common trap: Vestibulospinal (E) is the classic “extensor-facilitating” tract, so it's easy to misapply that same pattern to every extrapyramidal tract — rubrospinal specifically does the opposite, favoring flexors.

questions.stem: This course's slides note that although the rubrospinal system is sometimes included among the principal postural-control pathways, in humans it is considered to have little significance for this function. Which THREE pathways are instead named as the principal postural-control pathways in humans?
questions.explanation: Postural stabilization is described as an unconscious postural reflex mediated principally by the vestibulospinal, tectospinal, and reticulospinal pathways; the rubrospinal system is explicitly noted as “sometimes included” but likely insignificant for this function in humans. Common trap: Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (A, B, C) are voluntary, pyramidal pathways — postural control is specifically described in these slides as originating from extrapyramidal (involuntary) pathways, not the pyramidal system.

questions.stem: Which fissure of the cerebellum separates the anterior lobe from the posterior lobe?
questions.explanation: The primary fissure divides the anterior lobe from the posterior lobe of the cerebellum; the postero-lateral fissure separates the posterior lobe from the flocculonodular lobe. Common trap: The postero-lateral fissure (E) is a very close distractor since it's also a genuine cerebellar fissure — the key is which TWO lobes it separates (posterior vs. flocculonodular, not anterior vs. posterior).

questions.stem: Classified by evolutionary origin, the flocculonodular lobe is termed the archicerebellum, and its associated deep cerebellar nucleus is the:
questions.explanation: The archicerebellar (flocculonodular lobe/vestibulocerebellum) nuclei are the fastigial nuclei; the paleocerebellar nuclei are the medial dentate and emboliform nuclei, and the neocerebellar nuclei are the lateral dentate. Common trap: Lateral dentate (B) is the neocerebellar nucleus instead — easy to mix up the evolutionary tiers (archi/paleo/neo) with their corresponding deep nuclei if you don't carefully track medial-to-lateral progression.

questions.stem: The globose and emboliform nuclei of the cerebellum are collectively known as the:
questions.explanation: The globose and emboliform nuclei together are called the interposed nuclei (nucleus interpositus), situated between the fastigial nucleus medially and the dentate nucleus laterally. Common trap: “Vestibular nuclei” (E) is a plausible-sounding distractor since the cerebellum has extensive vestibular connections, but the vestibular nuclei are brainstem structures, not cerebellar deep nuclei at all.

questions.stem: Which cerebellar peduncle is the largest of the three, carrying pontocerebellar fibers (over 90% of its afferents) to reach the contralateral neocerebellar cortex?
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle is the largest of the three cerebellar peduncles; more than 90% of its fibers are pontocerebellar afferents, carrying the corticopontocerebellar pathway to the contralateral neocerebellum. Common trap: Restiform body and juxtarestiform body (D, E) are actually the two subdivisions of the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle, not separate peduncles of their own — a common naming trap.

questions.stem: Cerebellar disease classically causes patients to write with abnormally large, poorly controlled handwriting (macrographia) in an attempt to keep their writing legible — the opposite handwriting change from which other movement disorder?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar disease enlarges handwriting (macrographia) to compensate for poor motor control, which is explicitly described as the reverse of Parkinsonism, where handwriting characteristically shrinks progressively across a page (micrographia). Common trap: Huntington's disease (D) causes involuntary choreiform movements that could plausibly disrupt handwriting too, but the specific, classically-taught “opposite” pairing for this handwriting sign is with Parkinson's disease and its micrographia.

questions.stem: The tapetum, a component of the corpus callosum, forms part of the wall of which structure?
options: The third ventricle, via the massa intermedia
The posterior and inferior horns of the lateral ventricle
The fourth ventricle and its lateral recesses
The cerebral aqueduct of the midbrain
questions.explanation: The tapetum is formed by corpus callosum fibers that sweep around to form the roof and lateral wall of the posterior horn and the lateral wall of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. Common trap: The interventricular foramen (C) is a real ventricular landmark, but it's related to the fornix/caudate head region, not the corpus callosum's tapetum fibers.

questions.stem: The posterior commissure carries fibers from the pretectal nuclei that cross the midline to reach the parasympathetic (Edinger-Westphal) portion of the oculomotor nuclei bilaterally. This crossing is the anatomical basis for which clinical finding?
questions.explanation: Because pretectal fibers cross via the posterior commissure to reach BOTH Edinger-Westphal nuclei, shining light in one eye causes bilateral pupillary constriction — the direct response in the illuminated eye and the consensual response in the other eye. Common trap: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (A) is a real oculomotor disorder, but it results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, unrelated to the posterior commissure's pupillary role.

questions.stem: Which long association fiber bundle connects the frontal lobe to the temporal pole?
questions.explanation: The uncinate fasciculus is the long association fiber bundle that hooks around the lateral sulcus to connect the frontal lobe with the pole of the temporal lobe. Common trap: The cingulum (B) also connects the frontal lobe to temporal structures, but specifically to the parahippocampal and adjacent temporal cortex via a path beneath the cingulate gyrus, not to the temporal pole directly — an easy pair to mix up.

questions.stem: Layer VI of the neocortex sends its principal output to the:
options: Contralateral hemisphere via the corpus callosum
questions.explanation: Layer VI is the corticothalamic output layer, projecting back to the thalamus; layer V is the layer that sends output to the basal ganglia, brainstem, and spinal cord. Common trap: Basal ganglia, brainstem, and spinal cord (A, B, C) are all genuine cortical output destinations, but they are reached from layer V, not layer VI — the two output layers are easy to conflate.

questions.stem: Heterotypical isocortex is subdivided into granular and agranular types based on cytoarchitecture. The agranular cortex, which is thin on granular layers but rich in large pyramidal cells, corresponds anatomically to the:
questions.explanation: Agranular heterotypical isocortex corresponds to the motor cortex (primary motor area 4 and premotor area 6), which is thin on the input-receiving granular layer IV but thick with large pyramidal output neurons; granular cortex, by contrast, characterizes the primary sensory areas (vision, touch, hearing). Common trap: Primary visual, somatosensory, and auditory cortex (B, C, E) are all examples of the GRANULAR heterotypical type instead — granular cortex is thick with layer IV neurons receiving thalamic sensory input, the opposite profile from agranular motor cortex.

questions.stem: According to a well-known functional mapping of the insular cortex, which of the following is one of its four described functional zones?
questions.explanation: The insular cortex's four described functional zones are sensorimotor processing, chemosensory function, social-emotional processing, and cognitive functions. Common trap: Auditory relay and visual attention (B, D) are legitimate brain functions, but they belong to the medial/lateral geniculate nuclei and pulvinar respectively, not to the insular cortex's described functional map.

questions.stem: Which ability is classically attributed to the NON-dominant cerebral hemisphere, in contrast to the language and calculation functions of the dominant hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The non-dominant hemisphere is classically associated with spatial perception of three-dimensional objects, singing, and playing musical instruments, while the dominant hemisphere handles language (speech, writing) and calculation. Common trap: Writing and calculation (A, B) are both dominant-hemisphere functions — don't let “non-dominant” tempt you into picking any cognitive task at random; the specific contrast tested here is spatial/artistic versus verbal/computational.

questions.stem: Apraxia is best defined as:
options: Loss of the ability to recognize familiar faces (prosopagnosia)
Inability to perform learned movements despite intact strength and no paralysis
Loss of the ability to comprehend spoken language (Wernicke's aphasia)
Loss of voluntary eye movements (ocular motor apraxia)
Inability to identify an object by touch alone (astereognosis)
questions.explanation: Apraxia is the inability to carry out learned, purposeful movements despite intact motor power, sensation, and coordination — critically, it occurs in the ABSENCE of paralysis, distinguishing it from simple weakness. Common trap: Options A and E describe prosopagnosia and astereognosis respectively — both are real cortical deficits, but neither is apraxia, which is specifically about the loss of learned motor programming, not perception or recognition.

questions.stem: The neostriatum (caudate nucleus + putamen) is embryologically derived from the telencephalon, while the paleostriatum (pallidum, i.e., the globus pallidus) is derived from the:
questions.explanation: The globus pallidus (paleostriatum/pallidum) is embryologically derived from the diencephalon, unlike the caudate and putamen (neostriatum), which arise from the telencephalon — this embryological difference is why the globus pallidus is sometimes described as functionally and developmentally distinct from the rest of the striatum. Common trap: Mesencephalon (midbrain, option E) is a tempting choice since the substantia nigra (a closely related basal ganglia structure) IS a midbrain structure — but the globus pallidus itself is diencephalic, not mesencephalic.

questions.stem: The subthalamic nucleus (STN), described in this course as the largest lens-shaped nucleus of the diencephalon, is bordered medially by the:
questions.explanation: The STN's medial border is the hypothalamus; superiorly it borders the thalamus and lenticular fasciculus, inferiorly the ansa lenticularis and substantia nigra, and laterally the subthalamic fasciculus and lentiform nucleus. Common trap: Thalamus (A) is the SUPERIOR border of the STN, not the medial one — the four boundaries are easy to rotate incorrectly if you don't fix a consistent orientation.

questions.stem: The mnemonic ‘TRAP’ is used to remember the cardinal features of Parkinson's disease. What does the ‘A’ in TRAP stand for?
questions.explanation: TRAP stands for Tremor (at rest), Rigidity, Akinesia (or bradykinesia), and Postural instability — the four cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease. Common trap: Anosmia (A) is actually a real, well-documented EARLY non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease, which can make it a tempting choice — but it is not part of the TRAP motor mnemonic itself.

questions.stem: Basal ganglia movement disorders are broadly classified as hypokinetic or hyperkinetic based on which pathway is affected. Hypokinetic disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, result from lesions of the:
questions.explanation: Hypokinetic disorders (reduced movement, e.g., Parkinson's disease) are classified as resulting from direct pathway lesions/dysfunction, while hyperkinetic disorders (excess movement, e.g., chorea, hemiballismus, dystonia) result from indirect pathway lesions/dysfunction. Common trap: It's tempting to assume “indirect pathway” (which normally suppresses movement) should be linked to hypokinetic disorders when it is UNDERACTIVE — but this course's classification scheme pairs hypokinetic disorders with the direct pathway and hyperkinetic disorders with the indirect pathway.

questions.stem: Within the neostriatum, medium spiny neurons release GABA along with co-localized neuropeptides. Which of these neuropeptides is specifically associated with regulating nociception (pain processing) in the body?
questions.explanation: Enkephalin, co-released by a subset of GABAergic medium spiny neurons, is involved in regulating nociception; Substance P, released by a different subset of medium spiny neurons, is instead associated with mood, anxiety, and stress regulation. Common trap: Substance P (E) is the other major medium spiny neuron neuropeptide covered in this course, making it an easy point of confusion — remember enkephalin for pain, Substance P for mood/stress.

questions.stem: Unlike the posterior pituitary, the anterior pituitary has no direct nerve fiber connections from the hypothalamus. Instead, hypothalamic control of the anterior pituitary is achieved via the:
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary is controlled by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones carried through a specialized portal blood vessel network (the hypothalamohypophyseal portal system), not by direct neural connections. Common trap: The supraopticohypophyseal tract (C) is a real, direct NEURAL pathway — but it carries hormones (ADH, oxytocin) to the POSTERIOR pituitary, the opposite of what's being asked about here.

questions.stem: The paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei contain large (magnocellular) neurosecretory cells whose axons travel via the hypothalamohypophyseal tract to the posterior pituitary. Damage to this system classically produces:
questions.explanation: Damage to the magnocellular neurosecretory system (paraventricular/supraoptic nuclei or their tract to the posterior pituitary) causes ADH deficiency, resulting in diabetes insipidus — excessive, dilute urine production. Common trap: SIADH (C) is essentially the opposite problem — excess, not deficient, ADH activity — an easy pair to reverse under exam pressure.

questions.stem: The mammillary body sends efferent fibers via two distinct tracts: the mammillothalamic tract (to the anterior thalamic nucleus, part of the Papez circuit) and the mammillotegmental tract. The mammillotegmental tract instead projects to the:
options: Prefrontal cortex, via the precommissural fornix
Midbrain tegmentum, then the reticular formation
questions.explanation: The mammillotegmental tract projects from the mammillary body to the midbrain tegmentum, with onward connections to the reticular formation, and is thought to be involved in autonomic nervous system functions — distinct from the memory-related mammillothalamic tract. Common trap: Cingulate gyrus (D) is the ultimate destination of the Papez circuit's anterior thalamic relay (via the mammillothalamic tract), not the target of the mammillotegmental tract being asked about here.

questions.stem: A patient presents with sudden altered consciousness and fluctuating neurological status. Diffusion-weighted MRI reveals bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts. This presentation is classically associated with occlusion of the:
questions.explanation: The Artery of Percheron is a rare anatomical variant in which a single paramedian arterial trunk (arising from one posterior cerebral artery) supplies BOTH paramedian thalami and often the rostral midbrain; its occlusion classically causes bilateral thalamic infarction with altered consciousness and fluctuating neurological status, best identified on diffusion-weighted MRI. Common trap: Thalamogeniculate artery (B) supplies the posterior two-thirds of the thalamus unilaterally (the classic territory for Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome) — a different vessel and a different, unilateral clinical picture from the bilateral Artery of Percheron presentation.

questions.stem: A patient develops severe, delayed-onset, spontaneous burning pain with hyperalgesia and allodynia on one side of the body, months after a stroke. This presentation, sometimes called central post-stroke pain or Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, classically results from a lesion of which thalamic nuclei?
questions.explanation: Thalamic (Dejerine-Roussy) syndrome classically results from a vascular lesion of the VPL/VPM nuclei (most often via the thalamogeniculate artery, a branch of the PCA), causing contralateral sensory disturbance that can evolve into severe, delayed, spontaneous burning pain — the thalamus doesn't just relay sensation, it can also amplify pain perception. Common trap: Anterior nucleus (D) is a tempting “famous thalamic nucleus” distractor, but its damage causes memory impairment via Papez-circuit disruption, not a pain syndrome.

questions.stem: The intralaminar and centromedian thalamic nuclei are part of the nonspecific thalamic projection system and receive input from the brainstem reticular formation. Unlike most other thalamic nuclei, their primary projection target is the:
options: Diffuse projection to all six cortical layers equally
Caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus
questions.explanation: Rather than projecting broadly to the cerebral cortex like most other thalamic nuclei, the intralaminar and centromedian nuclei project primarily to the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus, functioning as part of the arousal system alongside the subthalamus and hypothalamus. Common trap: It's easy to assume any “nonspecific, diffusely-projecting” thalamic system must target the cortex broadly (as the reticular activating system does) — but this course specifically emphasizes that these particular nuclei project to the basal ganglia instead.

questions.stem: Bidirectional connections between the medial dorsal (mediodorsal) thalamic nucleus and the frontal lobe mean that damage to this nucleus can produce a frontal lobe syndrome with personality changes, as well as memory loss resembling which classic clinical syndrome?
questions.explanation: The medial dorsal (mediodorsal) nucleus has strong bidirectional links to the frontal lobe; damage produces frontal lobe personality changes as well as memory impairment resembling Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (classically attributed to mammillary body damage, but also linked to mediodorsal thalamic involvement). Common trap: Klüver-Bucy syndrome (B) is a tempting “famous syndrome” distractor, but it results from bilateral temporal lobe/amygdala damage, unrelated to the medial dorsal thalamic nucleus.

questions.stem: The lateral dorsal (LD) and lateral posterior (LP) thalamic nuclei are described as ‘integrative’ nuclei because, unusually for the thalamus, they:
options: Are the only thalamic nuclei with no cortical projection at all
Connect mainly with other thalamic nuclei, not a primary sensory pathway
Have no afferent connections of any kind
Receive input exclusively from the retina
Project exclusively to the cerebellar cortex
questions.explanation: The LD/LP nuclei are described as integrative because their connections are largely restricted to other thalamic nuclei (with reciprocal connections to the superior parietal cortex, areas 5 and 7), rather than relaying one specific, primary sensory or motor pathway the way VPL, VPM, or the geniculate bodies do. Common trap: Option A describes the reticular nucleus, a genuinely distinct thalamic nucleus with no cortical projection — a different “unusual” thalamic nucleus from the LD/LP pair being asked about here.

questions.stem: In the Papez circuit, hippocampal output leaves via the fornix and reaches the:
questions.explanation: The classic Papez circuit runs: hippocampus (via the subiculum) → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus (via the cingulum) → entorhinal cortex → back to the hippocampus. Fornix output specifically terminates at the mammillary bodies, the very next stop after leaving the hippocampus. Common trap: The anterior thalamic nucleus (B) is reached later in the circuit, via the mammillothalamic tract from the mammillary bodies, not directly from the fornix — it's easy to skip a step and jump straight to the more 'famous' thalamic relay.

questions.stem: Lesions of the septal area (septal nuclei) produce a syndrome useful to contrast with Klüver-Bucy syndrome, consisting of hyper-reactivity/irritability, amnesia, and:
questions.explanation: Septal nuclei lesions produce hyper-reactivity/irritability, amnesia, and hypersexuality — a distinct syndrome that is useful to contrast with Klüver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral temporal/amygdala damage), which also features hypersexuality but alongside hyperorality and psychic blindness rather than irritability. Common trap: Hyperorality and psychic blindness (C, E) are Klüver-Bucy features, not septal syndrome features — both syndromes share hypersexuality, which is exactly why this question tests the OTHER features that distinguish them.

questions.stem: Mitral and tufted cells are the principal projection (output) neurons of the olfactory bulb. What makes them functionally unique compared to output neurons of other sensory systems?
options: They synapse directly onto lower motor neurons in the spinal cord
They regenerate throughout life, unlike all other CNS projection neurons
They remain unmyelinated for their entire axonal length
They form the only olfactory relay to cortex, bypassing the thalamus
They are the only inhibitory output neurons in any sensory system
questions.explanation: Mitral and tufted cells are the sole relay carrying all olfactory information onward from the olfactory bulb (via the lateral olfactory tract to piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex) — and this pathway is unique among the senses in bypassing an obligatory thalamic relay before reaching cortex. Common trap: Option B describes the OLFACTORY RECEPTOR NEURONS (which do regenerate from basal cells), not the mitral/tufted output neurons of the bulb — an easy mix-up between two different cell populations in the same system.

questions.stem: The cardiac plexus has a superficial part (in the concavity of the aortic arch) and a deep part (at the bifurcation of the trachea). The superficial part is formed by contributions specifically from the:
options: Right sympathetic trunk and right vagus nerve only
Left sympathetic trunk, left vagus nerve, and left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve and left vagus nerve only
Bilateral vagus nerves only, with no sympathetic contribution at all
Bilateral sympathetic trunks only, with no vagal contribution at all
questions.explanation: The superficial part of the cardiac plexus is formed by the cervical cardiac branch of the LEFT sympathetic trunk, the cardiac branch of the LEFT vagus nerve, and the LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve; the deep part, by contrast, is formed by cardiac nerves from the cervical ganglia of the RIGHT sympathetic trunk and cardiac branches of the RIGHT vagus. Common trap: It's easy to assume the cardiac plexus is formed symmetrically from both sides equally, but this course specifically teaches a lateralized split — left-sided contributions form the superficial part, right-sided contributions form the deep part.

questions.stem: Most visceral effectors receive dual (both sympathetic and parasympathetic) innervation. Which of the following effectors receives sympathetic innervation ONLY, without any parasympathetic input?
questions.explanation: Sweat glands, along with the adrenal medulla, arrector pili muscles, and most blood vessels, receive sympathetic innervation only — they have no parasympathetic supply at all, unlike most other viscera, which receive dual innervation. Common trap: The heart, bladder, iris, and stomach (A, B, C, E) are all classic examples of DUAL innervation (with sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often working antagonistically or cooperatively) — sweat glands are the outlier without dual input.

questions.stem: The parotid gland receives its parasympathetic secretomotor innervation via the inferior salivatory nucleus, cranial nerve IX, the tympanic plexus, and finally synapses in the:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers for the parotid gland originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, travel via CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and the tympanic plexus, and synapse in the otic ganglion before reaching the gland — in contrast to the submandibular and sublingual glands, which are supplied via CN VII and the submandibular ganglion. Common trap: Submandibular ganglion (D) is the postganglionic relay for the SUBMANDIBULAR and SUBLINGUAL glands (via CN VII), not the parotid gland — a very commonly confused pairing among the salivary glands.

questions.stem: According to the three-neuron classification of Horner's syndrome taught in this course, a lesion of the FIRST-order neuron (between the brainstem and the cervicothoracic spinal cord) is most commonly caused by:
options: Stroke, such as lateral medullary syndrome
A neck mass or lymph node enlargement
questions.explanation: First-order Horner's syndrome lesions occur between the brainstem and the cervicothoracic spinal cord; stroke (classically lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome) is the most common cause, with space-occupying lesions, multiple sclerosis, and cervical cord trauma as other causes. Common trap: Pancoast tumor (D) is the classic cause of SECOND-order Horner's syndrome (affecting the preganglionic sympathetic fibers as they pass near the lung apex), not the first-order lesion being asked about here.

questions.stem: Continuing the three-neuron classification of Horner's syndrome, which cause is specifically associated with THIRD-order neuron lesions and is considered the most concerning to rule out?
questions.explanation: Third-order Horner's syndrome lesions occur along the postganglionic sympathetic fibers (from the superior cervical ganglion onward, traveling with the internal carotid artery); carotid artery dissection is the most concerning cause to exclude, given its risk of stroke, alongside neck masses as another recognized cause. Common trap: Pancoast tumor (E) is the classic SECOND-order cause, and lateral medullary syndrome (C) and multiple sclerosis/cervical trauma (B, D) are FIRST-order causes — keeping the three neuron orders straight is the main challenge in this question family.

questions.stem: Regarding autonomic effects on the gastrointestinal tract, which statement correctly pairs sympathetic stimulation with its effect?
options: Increases peristalsis, relaxes sphincters, increases glandular secretion
Decreases peristalsis, contracts sphincters, decreases glandular secretion
Has no effect on GI motility, only on secretion
Increases peristalsis but also contracts sphincters
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation of the GI tract decreases peristalsis, contracts sphincters, and decreases glandular secretion — consistent with its general “rest-interrupting,” activity-suppressing role in digestion; parasympathetic stimulation produces the opposite effects (increased peristalsis, relaxed sphincters, increased secretion). Common trap: Option B describes the PARASYMPATHETIC pattern — an easy full reversal if you mix up which division is being asked about.

questions.stem: At the sinoatrial node, sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate in part by opening the ‘funny’ (If) channels and T-type Ca2+ channels, which increases the slope of phase 4 of the pacemaker potential. Parasympathetic stimulation slows heart rate by shutting these channels down and additionally by:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation slows the SA node's pacemaker activity both by reducing funny-channel/T-type Ca2+ channel activity (flattening the phase 4 slope) and by opening K+ channels, which hyperpolarizes the pacemaker cell membrane and delays the next threshold crossing. Common trap: L-type Ca2+ channel opening (D) is actually part of the SYMPATHETIC mechanism, increasing contractility (not the parasympathetic slowing mechanism) — don't let “calcium channel” alone signal which autonomic division is involved.

questions.stem: Unlike the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle, under autonomic control), the EXTERNAL urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control. It is innervated by somatic motor fibers from the pudendal nerve, originating from a specialized sacral spinal cord nucleus called:
options: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
questions.explanation: Onuf's nucleus, a specialized somatic motor nucleus in the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4), innervates the external urethral and anal sphincters via the pudendal nerve, providing voluntary control over these skeletal muscle sphincters — distinct from the autonomic (smooth muscle) control of the internal sphincter and detrusor. Common trap: The intermediolateral cell column (D) is the location of PREGANGLIONIC AUTONOMIC (sympathetic) neurons, not the somatic motor neurons of Onuf's nucleus — an easy mix-up between autonomic and somatic sacral cell columns.

questions.stem: In the adrenal medulla, catecholamine output is a mixture of both hormones, with epinephrine making up the larger share. Approximately what proportion of adrenal medullary catecholamine output is epinephrine versus norepinephrine?
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines in an approximate ratio of 80% epinephrine to 20% norepinephrine, reflecting the PNMT-mediated conversion of most of the norepinephrine produced there into epinephrine before release. Common trap: Reversing the ratio (B) is the most common error — remember that the ADRENAL MEDULLA is specifically set up (via high local cortisol inducing PNMT) to convert the MAJORITY of its catecholamine output to epinephrine, unlike sympathetic nerve terminals elsewhere, which release norepinephrine almost exclusively.

questions.stem: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are subdivided into five types (M1–M5). Which muscarinic receptor subtype is located in the heart and mediates the slowing of heart rate by the vagus nerve?
questions.explanation: M2 muscarinic receptors are located in the heart and mediate vagally-induced slowing of heart rate; M3 receptors are found on glands and smooth muscle, while M1, M4, and M5 are located in the CNS. Common trap: M3 (A) is the receptor most students associate with parasympathetic effects generally (glands, smooth muscle, pupil, bladder), which makes it tempting here — but the heart specifically uses M2, a distinct subtype.

questions.stem: Delta waves (1–5 Hz) are a normal finding during deep sleep in adults and are also normal in awake infants. However, delta waves recorded in an AWAKE adult are considered:
options: A sign of enhanced cognitive performance
A normal variant with no clinical significance
questions.explanation: While delta waves are entirely normal during deep sleep and in awake infants, their presence in an awake ADULT is considered abnormal and indicates brain damage. Common trap: “Normal variant” (C) is tempting since delta waves ARE normal in some contexts (deep sleep, infancy) — but the specific context asked about here (an awake adult) is exactly the situation where delta waves lose their normal status.

questions.stem: The 2.5–3 Hz generalized spike-wave discharges seen on EEG during an absence seizure are believed to be generated by abnormal activity in which specific type of ion channel, located in thalamic neurons?
questions.explanation: The rhythmic 2.5–3 Hz spike-wave discharges of absence seizures are thought to arise from abnormal oscillatory activity generated by low-threshold T-type Ca2+ channels in thalamic (thalamocortical relay) neurons — the same channel type responsible for normal thalamic burst-firing during sleep spindle generation. Common trap: L-type Ca2+ channels (C) are the “long-lasting” cardiac/skeletal muscle-associated calcium channel type — a different channel family from the low-threshold, transient (‘T-type’) channels responsible for this specific thalamic oscillation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes sleep from coma?
options: Sleep is reversible with stimulation; coma is not arousable at all
There is no meaningful clinical or EEG distinction between sleep and coma
Coma always involves normal, regular REM sleep cycling, unlike sleep
Sleep involves complete, permanent loss of all brainstem reflexes
Sleep and coma are both permanent, completely unarousable states
questions.explanation: Sleep is defined as unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli; this is the key feature distinguishing it from coma, a state of unconsciousness from which the person cannot be aroused. Common trap: Option E collapses the very distinction the question is testing — sleep is specifically defined by its AROUSABILITY, which is exactly what separates it from coma.

questions.stem: During a typical 7- to 8-hour sleep period, REM sleep episodes recur at approximately what interval, gradually lengthening as the night progresses?
options: Only once, near the end of the sleep period
questions.explanation: REM sleep episodes recur approximately every 90 minutes during a normal night's sleep, with three to five episodes total, and each successive REM period tends to lengthen as the night progresses. Common trap: “Only once, near the end” (C) is a common misconception — REM sleep actually recurs multiple times throughout the night in a cyclical pattern, not just as a single late-night event.

questions.stem: Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan via a pathway that includes serotonin as an intermediate. Which enzyme in this pathway is specifically regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, via sympathetic (adrenergic) input, and is considered the pathway's regulated step?
questions.explanation: Arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) converts serotonin to N-acetylserotonin and is specifically regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus through adrenergic input from the sympathetic nervous system, making it the key controlled step in melatonin synthesis; HIOMT then completes the pathway by converting N-acetylserotonin to melatonin. Common trap: HIOMT (C) is the FINAL enzyme in the pathway (producing melatonin itself), which makes it a tempting “last step = regulated step” guess — but the SCN-regulated, rate-controlling step is specifically AANAT, one step earlier.

questions.stem: A patient's ankle reflex appears absent on initial testing. The examiner asks the patient to interlock the fingers of both hands and pull them apart forcefully while the reflex is retested, and the reflex becomes elicitable. This reinforcement technique is called:
questions.explanation: The Jendrassik maneuver is a reinforcement technique used when a deep tendon reflex is difficult to elicit: for lower limb reflexes, the patient interlocks and pulls apart the fingers of both hands; for upper limb reflexes, the patient clenches the teeth. Both actions increase gamma motor neuron activity, enhancing the reflex response. Common trap: The doll's eye maneuver and oculocephalic maneuver (A, E) are the same test (assessing the vestibulo-ocular reflex in an unconscious patient) but are unrelated to deep tendon reflex reinforcement.

questions.stem: Renshaw cells, located in the anterior horns of the spinal cord in close association with motor neurons, perform which function?
options: They serve as the primary afferent limb of the myotatic reflex
They directly innervate extrafusal muscle fibers
They locally synthesize and release dopamine as a transmitter
They carry proprioceptive information to the cerebellum
They provide recurrent inhibitory feedback to nearby motor neurons
questions.explanation: Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons that receive collateral input from motor neuron axons and feed back inhibitory signals onto the same and neighboring motor neurons — a recurrent inhibition circuit that helps regulate motor neuron firing rate and prevent excessive excitation. Common trap: Option A describes the Ia afferent fiber from the muscle spindle, a completely different component of the reflex arc from the Renshaw cell, which is a spinal interneuron, not a sensory afferent.

questions.stem: Reflexes can be classified along several axes. Along the ‘complexity’ axis, a reflex mediated through a single synapse between the afferent and efferent neuron is termed:
questions.explanation: Reflex classification includes an axis based on synaptic complexity: monosynaptic reflexes involve a single synapse (the classic example being the myotatic/stretch reflex), while polysynaptic reflexes involve multiple synapses (such as the withdrawal reflex). Common trap: “Cranial” (D) classifies reflexes by their PROCESSING SITE (brainstem vs. spinal cord), a completely different axis from the synaptic-complexity classification being asked about here.

questions.stem: In the inverse myotatic (Golgi tendon) reflex, type Ib afferents from the Golgi tendon organ synapse with Ib inhibitory interneurons upon entering the spinal cord. The effect of this inhibitory interneuron is to:
options: Inhibit the Golgi tendon organ itself, preventing further signaling
Inhibit alpha-motor output to the homonymous (agonist) muscle
Have no effect on either the homonymous or heteronymous muscle
Excite alpha-motor output to the homonymous (agonist) muscle
questions.explanation: The Ib inhibitory interneuron inhibits alpha-motor output to the homonymous (contracting) muscle whose tendon organ was stretched, while a separate, simultaneously-activated excitatory interneuron activates alpha-motor output to the heteronymous (antagonist) muscle — a reciprocal pattern that protects the muscle-tendon unit from excessive tension. Common trap: Option E describes the role of the EXCITATORY interneuron in this same circuit, which acts on the heteronymous muscle — the INHIBITORY interneuron specifically targets the homonymous muscle instead.

questions.stem: When light is shone into one eye, the pupillary light reflex causes both the ipsilateral (direct) and contralateral (consensual) pupils to constrict. This bilateral response occurs because pretectal neurons project to BOTH Edinger-Westphal nuclei via the:
questions.explanation: Pretectal neurons send crossing fibers via the posterior commissure to reach BOTH Edinger-Westphal nuclei, which is why stimulating one eye's pupillary light reflex produces bilateral pupillary constriction (direct and consensual responses). Common trap: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (E) coordinates conjugate EYE MOVEMENTS (its lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia), a completely different function from the posterior commissure's role in the bilateral pupillary light reflex.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: The central artery of the retina, a branch of the ophthalmic artery, is notable because it is the sole blood supply to the inner five layers of the retina and is described as a functional ‘end artery.’ What is the clinical consequence of its occlusion?
options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, from a post-chiasmal lesion
Permanent monocular blindness, with no collateral circulation
Transient, fully reversible blurring of vision
No visual consequence, since the outer retinal layers compensate
questions.explanation: Because the central retinal artery is an end artery supplying the only blood source to the inner five retinal layers, with no significant collateral circulation, its occlusion results in permanent blindness of the affected eye — a true ophthalmologic emergency. Common trap: Bitemporal and homonymous hemianopia (A, B) are visual field defects from lesions further along the visual pathway (chiasm and post-chiasmal structures, respectively), not from a retinal end-artery occlusion, which causes monocular blindness instead.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: The anterior choroidal artery, a direct branch of the internal carotid artery, supplies a wide territory including the hippocampus, amygdala, optic tract, lateral geniculate body, and globus pallidus, as well as the proximal portion of the optic radiations as they leave the lateral geniculate body to form the:
questions.explanation: The anterior choroidal artery supplies the proximal portion of the optic radiations as they sweep from the lateral geniculate body into the temporal lobe to form Meyer's loop, in addition to its other deep structure territory (hippocampus, amygdala, optic tract, globus pallidus). Common trap: Arcuate fasciculus (A) sounds similar to “Meyer's loop” in a memory-recall sense (both being curved white matter pathways), but the arcuate fasciculus connects Broca's and Wernicke's areas and has nothing to do with the visual radiations.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are small microaneurysms of the tiny penetrating vessels that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule, and are the classic underlying lesion in hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. These microaneurysms most commonly affect which arteries?
options: Ophthalmic artery and its retinal branches
questions.explanation: Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms classically affect the lenticulostriate (lateral striate) arteries — small penetrating branches of the MCA that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule — and their rupture, typically in the setting of chronic hypertension, is the classic cause of hypertensive intracerebral (basal ganglia) hemorrhage. Common trap: Anterior choroidal artery (B) also supplies deep structures and can be confused with the lenticulostriate arteries, but the classic Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm site is specifically the small MCA lenticulostriate perforators, not the anterior choroidal artery.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: A patient develops contralateral hemiparesis together with ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) palsy after a stroke affecting the midbrain, a territory supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. This classic brainstem syndrome is called:
questions.explanation: Weber's syndrome results from a midbrain lesion (PCA territory) affecting the cerebral peduncle (causing contralateral hemiparesis, since corticospinal fibers haven't yet crossed) together with the exiting fascicles of CN III (causing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy). Common trap: Millard-Gubler syndrome (E) is a similarly-patterned crossed brainstem syndrome, but it occurs at the level of the PONS (involving CN VI and/or VII with contralateral hemiparesis), not the midbrain — an easy syndrome to confuse with Weber's due to the shared “crossed” pattern.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the cranium through the foramen spinosum and runs between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura. Laceration of this artery (classically from a temporal bone fracture) results in:
questions.explanation: Because the middle meningeal artery runs in the potential space between the periosteal and meningeal dural layers (not within the subdural or subarachnoid spaces), its laceration produces an epidural hematoma — classically following a temporal bone fracture that tears the artery as it grooves the inner skull table. Common trap: Subdural hematoma (C) instead results from tearing of the bridging veins that cross the subdural space — a venous, often slower-developing bleed, in contrast to the arterial, rapidly-expanding epidural hematoma from middle meningeal artery injury.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid within the subarachnoid space is reabsorbed into the venous blood of the superior sagittal sinus through small projections of arachnoid mater called:
options: Choroid plexus villi within the ventricles
Denticulate ligaments of the spinal dura
Pacchionian folds of the inner dura
questions.explanation: Arachnoid granulations (also called arachnoid villi) are projections of arachnoid mater that protrude into the superior sagittal sinus, allowing CSF to be reabsorbed from the subarachnoid space into the venous blood. Common trap: Arachnoid trabeculae (D) are the fine strands of connective tissue spanning the subarachnoid space itself (supporting blood vessels and maintaining space), not the structures responsible for CSF reabsorption into venous blood.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) receives blood from the internal cerebral veins and the basal vein (of Rosenthal), and then drains into the:
options: Inferior sagittal sinus (before the straight sinus)
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein of Galen receives the paired internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal, then drains directly into the straight sinus, which subsequently joins the confluence of sinuses. Common trap: The inferior sagittal sinus (B) does join the straight sinus too (carrying blood from the falx cerebri), but it does so as a SEPARATE tributary alongside the great cerebral vein, not by receiving the great cerebral vein's drainage before passing it along.

questions.section: Lecture 28 — Blood Supply of Brain & Meninges
questions.stem: A stroke in the posterior cerebral artery territory characteristically produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, but with a distinctive feature not typically seen with MCA-territory visual field loss: the finding is called:
questions.explanation: PCA-territory occipital lobe infarcts classically spare the macula (central vision) due to collateral blood supply to the occipital pole from MCA branches, producing a homonymous hemianopia ‘with macular sparing’ — a distinguishing feature from other causes of homonymous visual field loss. Common trap: Complete monocular blindness (E) describes an END-ARTERY retinal or optic nerve problem (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion), not the partial, macula-sparing homonymous field defect characteristic of PCA-territory cortical strokes.

questions.stem: Along the spectrum of decreasing alertness, a patient who falls asleep unless repeatedly stimulated, but who has little to no spontaneous activity when awakened, is best described as:
questions.explanation: The consciousness spectrum runs Alert → Confused (disoriented, impaired thinking) → Somnolent (falls asleep without repeated stimulation) → Stuporous (a sleep-like state with little or no spontaneous activity, requiring vigorous/repeated stimulation to arouse) → Comatose (cannot be aroused at all). Common trap: Somnolent (D) is a very close, commonly confused neighbor — the key distinguishing detail here is the description of needing REPEATED stimulation and having little spontaneous activity even when aroused, which specifically describes the stuporous level, one step deeper than somnolence.

questions.stem: Using the classification of aphasia by fluency, comprehension, and repetition, a patient with FLUENT speech, INTACT comprehension, but IMPAIRED repetition has which type of aphasia?
questions.explanation: Conduction aphasia is characterized by fluent speech and intact comprehension, but disproportionately impaired repetition — classically attributed to a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus disconnecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas. Common trap: Anomic aphasia (E) also features fluent speech and intact comprehension, but with intact (not impaired) repetition — its hallmark deficit is word-finding difficulty (anomia), not the repetition problem being described here.

questions.stem: A patient can neither read nor write, and the lesion is localized to the left angular gyrus. This presentation is termed:
questions.explanation: Alexia with agraphia (combined inability to read AND write) localizes to the left angular gyrus — in contrast to alexia WITHOUT agraphia (can't read but can still write), which instead results from a lesion of the medial left occipital cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum (or left lateral geniculate body and splenium). Common trap: Alexia WITHOUT agraphia (B) is the classic disconnection syndrome from a splenium/occipital lesion — the key distinguishing detail here is that this patient cannot read OR write, pointing to the angular gyrus lesion instead.

questions.stem: Gerstmann syndrome results from a lesion of the angular gyrus in the dominant (usually left) parietal lobe. Which of the following is NOT one of the four classic components of Gerstmann syndrome?
options: Finger agnosia (inability to name the fingers)
questions.explanation: The four classic components of Gerstmann syndrome are acalculia, finger agnosia, agraphia, and left-right confusion. Prosopagnosia (face blindness) is a distinct deficit associated instead with damage to the nondominant inferior temporal lobe's face-recognition area, not with Gerstmann syndrome. Common trap: Because prosopagnosia is also a ‘recognition’-type cortical deficit, it's easy to lump it in with the other Gerstmann features — but it is anatomically and clinically a separate entity from the angular gyrus tetrad.

questions.stem: A patient understands what needs to be done and has intact strength and coordination, but cannot translate the idea of a learned action (such as pretending to use a comb) into the correct sequence of motor commands to actually perform it. This specific apraxia subtype is called:
questions.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia is the inability to convert a correctly understood idea about how to perform an action into the actual motor plan needed to execute it — the patient knows WHAT to do but cannot translate that knowledge into the correct movements. Common trap: Ideational apraxia (E) sounds similar but is a distinct deficit: an inability to even CONCEIVE the correct idea/sequence of how to perform an action in the first place, leading to errors in the plan itself, not just its motor execution.

questions.stem: The meninges are functionally divided into the pachymeninges (the dura mater) and the leptomeninges (the pia and arachnoid together). Infectious (e.g., bacterial) meningitis predominantly affects which layer?
options: Neither layer, only the underlying brain parenchyma
questions.explanation: Infectious meningitis predominantly affects the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid), while granulomatous or chronic inflammatory processes (such as tuberculosis or fungal infections) more often involve the pachymeninges (dura), although exceptions exist in both directions. Common trap: It's easy to assume ‘meningitis’ (an infection OF the meninges) must affect whichever layer is thickest/most prominent (the dura), but the classically-taught pattern specifically pairs acute infectious meningitis with the thinner leptomeningeal layers.

questions.stem: During color vision testing in a patient with a suspected optic neuropathy, which color is classically the first to show reduced perception (appearing washed out or ‘desaturated’ compared to the unaffected eye)?
questions.explanation: In neurological (optic nerve) conditions, red color perception is classically lost first; red normally appears brighter in the center of the visual field than off-center, and a reversal of this pattern suggests impairment of central vision. Common trap: Blue (D) is sometimes cited as an early loss in certain non-neurological conditions (e.g., some inherited or lens-related color vision changes), but for OPTIC NERVE/neurological conditions specifically, this course teaches that red is lost first.

questions.stem: During a swinging flashlight test, one pupil is observed to paradoxically DILATE (rather than constrict) when the light is swung from the normal eye to the affected eye. This finding, called a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD or Marcus Gunn pupil), localizes the lesion to the:
questions.explanation: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) localizes to the optic nerve (CN II) on the affected side — the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is weakened, so swinging the light onto the affected eye produces a paradoxical dilation rather than the expected constriction. Common trap: CN III (D) is the tempting choice since it's the classic ‘pupil nerve,’ but CN III palsies cause a FIXED, DILATED pupil unresponsive to light in general (affecting the efferent limb), not the specific relative, swinging-light pattern of an afferent defect.

questions.stem: When comparing air conduction (AC) and bone conduction (BC) with a tuning fork (Rinne test), the NORMAL finding in a person with intact hearing is that:
options: Air conduction is heard louder and longer than bone conduction
The sound lateralizes to one ear
Neither air nor bone conduction is perceived
Air and bone conduction are perceived as exactly equal
Bone conduction is heard louder and longer than air conduction
questions.explanation: In the normal Rinne test, air conduction (AC) is louder and heard longer than bone conduction (BC) — an abnormal (‘Rinne-negative’) result, where BC is louder than AC, suggests a conductive hearing loss on that side. Common trap: Option B describes a feature of the WEBER test, not the Rinne test — a normal Weber test is NOT lateralized (heard equally/centrally), while an abnormal Weber test does lateralize; don't conflate the two related but distinct tuning-fork tests.

questions.stem: Within the vestibular labyrinth, the utricle and saccule respond primarily to linear acceleration (and static head position relative to gravity), while the three semicircular canals respond primarily to:
options: Static head position relative to gravity only
Linear acceleration in a straight line
questions.explanation: The three semicircular canals are specialized to detect angular acceleration — rotational movements of the head in the planes of the canals — while the utricle and saccule (the otolith organs) detect linear acceleration and static head tilt relative to gravity. Common trap: “Static head position only” (A) actually describes part of the utricle/saccule's job, not the semicircular canals' — the canals are specifically dynamic, rotation-detecting structures, not static-position sensors.

questions.stem: Cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal) is difficult to test in isolation because most of its functions overlap with other nerves. However, one muscle receives its motor innervation purely from CN IX and no other nerve. That muscle is the:
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus is the one muscle that receives its motor innervation purely from CN IX (glossopharyngeal nerve), making it the only muscle whose isolated weakness would specifically implicate a pure CN IX motor lesion. Common trap: Palatoglossus (D) is a tempting distractor given its tongue/palate-related name, but it is actually innervated by CN X (vagus, via the pharyngeal plexus), not CN IX.

questions.stem: The vagus nerve (CN X) is described as the longest and most widely distributed cranial nerve. The most common cause of unilateral vocal cord paralysis is a lesion of the:
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus that loops back up to innervate the larynx, is the most common site of injury leading to unilateral vocal cord paralysis — clinically important given its long course and proximity to structures in the neck and chest (e.g., thyroid surgery, mediastinal masses, aortic arch aneurysms). Common trap: Superior laryngeal nerve injury (A) instead causes more subtle voice changes (loss of high-pitched phonation, weak cricothyroid) rather than the frank vocal cord paralysis caused by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

questions.stem: Cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue with one specific exception. Which tongue muscle is NOT innervated by CN XII?
questions.explanation: CN XII supplies every intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscle except the palatoglossus, which is innervated by CN X (vagus, via the pharyngeal plexus) despite being a tongue muscle by location — a classic exception worth memorizing. Common trap: Genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus (A, B, D) are all classic CN XII-innervated extrinsic tongue muscles — palatoglossus is the one true exception among the tongue musculature.

questions.stem: During visual acuity testing, a patient's vision improves when they view the Snellen chart through a pinhole occluder. This improvement suggests that the patient's visual impairment is most likely due to:
options: A refractive error, rather than a neurological cause
A homonymous hemianopia from a post-chiasmal lesion
An optic chiasm compression from a pituitary mass
A lesion of the optic nerve itself
A lesion of the occipital visual cortex
questions.explanation: Improvement of visual acuity when looking through a pinhole occluder suggests that the underlying problem is a refractive error (correctable by optics) rather than a neurological cause — the pinhole eliminates most of the effect of refractive error by narrowing the bundle of light rays entering the eye. Common trap: Optic nerve, occipital cortex, chiasm, and homonymous hemianopia (B, C, D, E) are all neurological causes of visual impairment that would NOT be expected to improve with a pinhole — the pinhole test is specifically useful for distinguishing refractive from neurological visual loss.

questions.stem: Hemineglect (unilateral neglect) is a lack of attention to events and actions occurring on one half of space, despite intact primary sensory pathways. It is classically most prominent and long-lasting after damage to which side/lobe?
questions.explanation: Hemineglect is classically most prominent and long-lasting after damage to the right (non-dominant) parietal lobe; patients may fail to attend to, or even deny ownership of, the contralateral (left) side of their body or visual field, sometimes failing to bathe or shave that side. Common trap: It's tempting to assume any given cortical deficit is worse with DOMINANT (usually left) hemisphere damage, since that side gets most of the emphasis in language-related teaching — but neglect is specifically a NON-dominant (right) hemisphere-predominant syndrome.
